name: Mingrelian
confidence_why: Borise 2020 and Poniava 2020 both report that the placement of Megrelian stress is contested, and the first-hand descriptions disagree on where main stress falls in words longer than two syllables: Kipshidze 1914 gives primary initial stress, Kluge 1916 penultimate, Gudava 1969 a penult/antepenult window for the Senaki dialect with contrastive pairs, Kiria, Ezugbaia, Memishishi and Chukhua 2015 t…

new_statements.quote: Stress properties of Megrelian are contested (though cf. Senaki Megrelian facts in section 4.2). [...] There is agreement in the literature that in disyllabic words stress is initial. Kluge (1916: 3) claims that in longer words stress is penultimate, and accompanied by high tone. According to Kipshidze (1914: 13), longer words have two stresses, primary on the initial syllable and secondary on either the penult (in four syllable words) or the antepenult (in longer ones). Final vowels in Megrelian are often lengthened, especially in the Zugdidi dialect (Gudava 1969: 109), which has also been analyzed as final stress (Tsagareli 1880: 7; Kiziria 1967: 65).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mingrelian (src StressTyp2) carries an empty rule, so nothing to agree or contradict with; Borise supplies the content: contested placement, initial stress agreed only for disyllables, a penult/antepenult window (C-final = penult, V-final = antepenult) for the Senaki dialect, plus secondary stress and verb-form exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Borise files Megrelian under 'conflicting descriptions': the only point of agreement is initial stress in disyllables; for longer words the sources diverge (Kluge: penult with high tone; Kipshidze: primary initial + secondary penult/antepenult; Tsagareli/Kiziria: final, which may really be final-vowel lengthening). The one dialect she describes as a system (Senaki, after Gudava 1969, §4.2 p. 8) is a penult/antepenult stress window: penultimate stress in consonant-final words, antepenultimate in vowel-final words, which she groups with quantity-sensitive stress-window systems (fn. 6 compares it to the Greek recessive accent).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Reported second-hand from Kipshidze (1914: 13): primary on the initial syllable, secondary on the penult in four-syllable words and on the antepenult in longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Senaki dialect (p. 8): some vowel-final verbs, including perfective future and certain aorist forms, keep penultimate stress, giving minimal pairs dóɣuru 'die.AOR.3SG' vs doɣúru 'die.PRF.FUT.3SG' (Gudava 1969: 109). Negative/prohibitive morphemes obligatorily attract stress (p. 11, citing Kluge 1916: 4). Stress is acoustically weak with much interspeaker variation; Samurzakano Megrelian stress is the strongest acoustically (p. 23).
new_statements.identity_note: Borise's stress-window statement is for the Senaki dialect of Megrelian (after Gudava 1969); final-stress analyses concern the Zugdidi dialect (final-vowel lengthening); Samurzakano Megrelian is noted only for acoustically stronger stress. Kluge 1916 and Kipshidze 1914 are not dialect-specified in Borise's summary.

readall_conflicts: Borise 2020 (p. 23) herself reports the disagreement: the literature agrees only that disyllables are stressed initially; for longer words Kluge 1916 gives penultimate stress (with high tone), Kipshidze 1914 gives primary initial stress with a secondary stress on the penult (4 syllables) or antepenult (5+), and Tsagareli 1880 / Kiziria 1967 analyse the lengthened final vowel (especially Zugdidi) as final stress; Gudava 1969 for the Senaki dialect gives a penult/antepenult window (penult if consonant-final, antepenult if vowel-final) with verb-form exceptions. Kluge 1916 itself could not be opened, so its claim rests on Borise's paraphrase. Poniava 2020 (already held by the project in the same folder from an earlier reading, not in this work list) adds an experimental result of initial stress in 2-3 syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words and second-syllable primary stress with a penult/antepenult secondary in 5-7 syllable words, which again differs from Kluge's penult.

audit.reasoning: Coding of record: excluded (undetermined-sources) after the first check showed StressTyp2's 'initial primary + 3R secondary' misreads its own source. Verified on held pages: Klimov 1999 p. 54 says the mirror image (2-3σ initial; polysyllables MAIN stress antepenult, SECONDARY initial; stress 'weakly expressed'); Harris 1991 §1.3 (Gudava 1969, Senak) gives a right-edge C-final-penult / V-final-antepenult rule with contrastive pairs and 'considerable variation'; Kipshidze 1914 §7 p. 013 (held, read on the page image) gives antepenult but alternatively a double stress with the MAIN stress word-initial, and calls the stress very weak outside interrogatives. sources.quote: p. 33 (abstract): 'In the scientific literature there is no common view regarding the position and nature of stress in Megrelian. Our study is based on experimental analysis. The experiment has revealed that in Megrelian, in two-syllable and three-syllable words the stress is on the initial syllable. However, in some case the stress falls on the penultimate syllable in three-syllable words. As for four-syllable words, the stress is on the antepenult though our experiment did not confirm the presence of the secondary stress. In five-syllable words the primary stress falls on the second syllable

sources.note: The only instrumental study of Megrelian word stress (18 speakers, 9 municipalities); states outright that the literature has no common view and finds weak stress with a length-dependent locus (σ1 at 2-3σ, σ2 at 4-7σ) matching none of Kipshidze/Klimov/Gudava/StressTyp2 — the quotable modern authority for the exclusion, which currently carries no quote at all.
